title: Customer Security Questionnaire Answer Draft — RBAC v2, Audit Logs, Retention, Admin Controls (v0.7)
content:
Doc status: DRAFT answer bank for enterprise security questionnaires. This is written to be copy/paste friendly and should be tailored to the specific customer and deployment mode (Hosted API vs Dedicated vs Private). Some details (e.g., internal service names, exact retention defaults, incident references) may be shared under NDA.

Last updated: 2025-03-06 (inputs from Security Eng + Audit Logging). Owner: Olga Petrov (GRC). Questions/edits: @Marcus Lin for authz details; @Kevin Osei for audit log/SIEM; @David Kim for SSO/IdP mapping; @Fiona McCarthy for break-glass monitoring/alerting.

============================================================
SECTION 1 — RBAC MODEL / LEAST PRIVILEGE
============================================================

Q: Do you support Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)?
A: Yes. Redwood Inference supports RBAC across our Console/admin tooling, API Gateway, and control plane services. RBAC is used to enforce least-privilege access for administrative and operational actions such as API key management, role/user management, audit log export, deployment operations (Dedicated/Private), routing policy changes, and model rollout controls.

Q: How granular is your RBAC? Is it limited to coarse roles (e.g., Admin/User), or can permissions be fine-grained?
A: RBAC is permission-based (fine-grained). Permissions are defined as explicit “action on resource” capabilities. Roles are collections of permissions; users (or groups) receive role bindings at a defined scope.

Q: What are RBAC primitives (permissions, roles, role bindings, scopes)?
A:
- Permission: An atomic authorization capability (e.g., “rotate API keys”, “export audit logs”, “edit routing policies”).
- Role: A named set of permissions (e.g., Security Admin, Billing Admin, Read-only Auditor, Deployment Operator).
- Role binding: Assigns a role to a subject (user, service identity, or mapped IdP group) at a particular scope.
- Scope: The boundary within which the role applies. Scope is designed to support org-level and (where applicable) narrower scopes such as project/environment/cluster, depending on product area and deployment mode.

Q: What scopes are supported (org / project / environment / cluster)?
A: Redwood’s RBAC supports organizational scoping and additional scoping for environments and clusters where relevant (notably Dedicated and Private operations). For example, a Private Deployment Operator can be scoped to a specific cluster, while an Auditor can be scoped to an organization or environment depending on the audit log partitioning model in that deployment.

Q: Can you restrict admin actions by environment (prod vs non-prod)?
A: Yes. Where environments are modeled (e.g., Dedicated/Private deployments), we support scoping role bindings to the environment/cluster so that operational privileges can be limited to non-production or specific clusters.

Q: Do you support separation of duties (SoD) / admin segmentation?
A: Yes. We provide role templates intended to separate duties, such as:
- Security Admin (e.g., user/role management, audit configuration)
- Deployment Operator (e.g., operational actions on Dedicated/Private clusters)
- Billing Admin (billing and invoices only)
- Read-only Auditor (read-only access to audit logs and configuration state)
Customers can further tailor roles to meet internal SoD requirements.

Q: Can custom roles be created?
A: Yes. Customers can create custom roles by selecting explicit permissions. We also provide built-in role templates that can be used as-is or cloned and modified.

Q: Is the authorization model “deny by default”?
A: Yes. Administrative/control plane actions are enforced using deny-by-default permission checks. Requests without an explicit allow (via role binding at the relevant scope) are denied.

Q: Do you support “break-glass” emergency admin access?
A: Yes. Break-glass access is supported for emergency scenarios with time-bound elevation and enhanced monitoring. Break-glass actions are explicitly logged, and the process includes approvals and post-use review. We can align with customer-specific approval workflows for Private deployments.

Q: How do you prevent permission drift or accidental privilege escalation?
A: We implement:
- Explicit permission catalog with validation/linting (uniqueness and naming conventions).
- Role templates with documented intent.
- Audit logging of role/permission changes (who changed what, when).
- Optional internal controls such as approval workflows for privileged changes (customer-specific for Private deployments).

Q: Do you support least privilege for API keys / service accounts?
A: Yes. API access uses scoped credentials and permission checks at the gateway and/or service layer. Administrative API keys can be constrained via role bindings and are not implicitly “superuser.”

Q: Are authorization checks consistently enforced across UI and API?
A: Yes. We enforce authorization server-side for both UI and API access paths. The Console does not rely on client-side enforcement; all sensitive actions are verified at request time.

Q: Where are authorization checks enforced (gateway vs service)?
A: Authorization enforcement follows a defense-in-depth model:
- API Gateway enforces permission checks for protected routes.
- Backend services also enforce checks for sensitive operations to prevent bypass from internal callers or misrouted traffic.
The enforcement pattern is standardized via shared middleware/interceptors and endpoint annotations.

Q: Can a user see why access was denied?
A: Yes. We provide structured denial reasons for administrators and support workflows. By default, end users receive a safe “permission denied” response. For administrators (and in approved troubleshooting scenarios), the platform can surface a “why denied” code/path that indicates which permission was missing and at what scope. (Exact behavior may depend on tenant settings and deployment mode.)

============================================================
SECTION 2 — IDENTITY, SSO, AND GROUP-TO-ROLE MAPPING
============================================================

Q: Do you support SSO / SAML / OIDC?
A: Redwood supports enterprise SSO integrations. RBAC operates as the authorization layer on top of authenticated identities.

Q: Can roles be assigned to IdP groups (e.g., Okta/Entra groups)?
A: Yes. Customers can map IdP groups to Redwood roles through role bindings. This supports centralized identity lifecycle management (joiners/movers/leavers) while keeping authorization least-privilege and auditable.

Q: How are privilege changes handled when a user changes groups?
A: Group membership changes in the customer IdP affect the effective roles/permissions. We also log authorization-relevant administrative changes within Redwood (e.g., role template changes, direct role bindings). For Private deployments, we can align the sync/refresh behavior to customer operational requirements.

Q: Do you support MFA for administrative access?
A: MFA enforcement is typically handled via the customer’s IdP (SSO). For Redwood-managed accounts (where applicable), we support MFA policies for Console access. (Confirm exact configuration per deployment mode during implementation.)

============================================================
SECTION 3 — AUDIT LOGGING (INCLUDING AUTHORIZATION DECISIONS)
============================================================

Q: Do you provide audit logs?
A: Yes. Redwood provides audit logs for security-relevant actions across Console and administrative/control plane APIs, including identity and access changes and operational/deployment changes.

Q: Are RBAC/authorization events included in audit logs?
A: Yes. Audit log events include authorization context for relevant actions. We capture the subject (who), the action/permission evaluated (what), the resource/scope (where), the decision (allow/deny), and supporting policy metadata (e.g., policy version identifier).

Q: Do you log denied authorization attempts?
A: Yes, for protected actions we can log authorization decisions including denies. This supports detection of misconfigurations, attempted unauthorized access, and incident investigations. Customers can tune alerting/monitoring around unusual deny rates.

Q: What fields are included in audit logs?
A: Typical fields include (exact schema may vary by deployment mode):
- Timestamp
- Actor/subject identity (user/service), plus org/tenant
- Action and permission identifier
- Resource identifiers and scope (org/project/env/cluster where applicable)
- Decision: allow/deny
- Denial reason code (where applicable)
- Request metadata (e.g., request id / trace id), source IP/UA when available
- Policy/version metadata (policy bundle version or equivalent)
- Target object metadata for mutating actions (e.g., role id changed, key id rotated)

Q: Are audit logs immutable / tamper-evident?
A: Redwood treats audit logs as security telemetry and restricts modification/deletion capabilities. In Hosted/Dedicated, audit logs are stored in managed systems with controlled access and integrity protections. In Private, audit logs are stored within the customer-controlled environment; customers can apply their own immutability controls (e.g., WORM storage, SIEM ingestion, log retention policies).

Q: Can audit logs be exported to a SIEM?
A: Yes. Audit logs can be exported and integrated with SIEMs. Export includes authorization decision context (subject/action/scope/decision and policy metadata) to support correlation and evidence requirements.

Q: Do you support near-real-time streaming of audit logs?
A: Depending on deployment mode and customer configuration, audit logs can be exported on a scheduled basis or near-real-time. For Private deployments, customers can integrate with their preferred log collection pipeline.

Q: Can you provide sample audit log entries for RBAC decisions?
A: Yes, under NDA if requested. We can provide representative examples showing role changes, role binding changes, API key rotation, routing policy edits, and audit log export events, including the authorization decision context.

Q: Are administrative actions (role creation, permission changes, role assignment) audited?
A: Yes. Role/permission administration events are audited, including who performed the change and what was changed.

============================================================
SECTION 4 — LOG RETENTION, DATA RESIDENCY, AND EXPORT CONTROLS
============================================================

Q: What is your audit log retention period?
A: Redwood supports configurable audit log retention. Default retention and maximum configurable windows depend on the customer plan and deployment mode. For Private deployments, retention is customer-controlled. For Hosted/Dedicated, Redwood can offer retention options aligned to enterprise requirements.

Q: Can the customer configure log retention and deletion?
A: Retention settings are configurable based on deployment mode and plan. Any capabilities to modify retention or delete logs are protected by explicit permissions and are audited.

Q: Do you support data residency requirements (e.g., EU-only storage)?
A: Redwood supports deployment options and region selection. For Private deployments, data residency is governed by the customer’s infrastructure choices. For Hosted/Dedicated, residency controls depend on region availability and contract terms.

Q: Can you restrict who can export audit logs?
A: Yes. Audit log export is a sensitive action protected by explicit permissions. We also recommend a separation-of-duties model where an Auditor can view but not export, and a Security Admin can export (or vice versa), depending on customer policy.

Q: Do you log audit export events?
A: Yes. Audit log export events are audited, including actor identity, time, scope, and export destination/format metadata when available.

============================================================
SECTION 5 — ADMIN CONTROLS / OPERATIONAL SAFEGUARDS
============================================================

Q: How do you control access to highly privileged functions (e.g., managing org admins, changing routing policies, modifying Private deployment settings)?
A: These actions require explicit high-sensitivity permissions. We provide role templates that isolate these permissions to specific administrator personas. We recommend limiting assignment counts and using IdP group mappings plus approvals for changes.

Q: Do you support approval workflows for privileged changes?
A: Redwood can align with customer approval workflows via operational processes (and for Private deployments, via customer tooling). At a minimum, privileged changes are auditable and can be monitored/alerted.

Q: Do you provide alerting on suspicious activity (e.g., repeated permission denied events, unusual role changes)?
A: Redwood supports telemetry and monitoring for authorization events (allow/deny rates, error codes) and audit log consumption by customer monitoring systems. For Private deployments, customers can implement alerting in their environment; Redwood can provide recommended detectors and dashboards.

Q: Can you restrict admin access by IP allowlist / network controls?
A: Network-level controls depend on deployment mode:
- Hosted/Dedicated: options may include IP allowlisting and secure access patterns depending on plan.
- Private: customer controls network boundaries and can enforce IP restrictions and private networking as required.

============================================================
SECTION 6 — EVIDENCE FOR SOC 2 / AUDITS / QUESTIONNAIRES
============================================================

Q: Can you provide documentation of your RBAC design and controls?
A: Yes. We can provide design documentation describing the RBAC model, permission catalog approach, enforcement points, audit logging schema, and operational controls (including break-glass). We can also provide test evidence and change management records upon request.

Q: Do you test authorization enforcement?
A: Yes. We maintain automated tests for critical permissions and protected routes, including integration tests for high-sensitivity operations (e.g., role changes, key rotation, routing policy edits). We also use coverage/guardrails to reduce risk of shipping unprotected sensitive endpoints.

Q: How do you handle backward compatibility / migration when authorization changes?
A: We use staged rollout mechanisms (feature flags, dual-read where appropriate) and monitor for deny spikes and customer impact. Changes are coordinated with release processes and documented for affected customers (especially Dedicated/Private).

============================================================
SECTION 7 — DEPLOYMENT-MODE SPECIFICS (HOSTED vs DEDICATED vs PRIVATE)
============================================================

Q: Does RBAC work the same in Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments?
A: The RBAC semantics are consistent across deployment modes (permissions, roles, bindings, scopes). Deployment modes differ primarily in operational ownership and integration points:
- Hosted API: Redwood operates the platform; customers manage org/users/roles and use audit log export/integration.
- Dedicated: Similar semantics with additional operational constructs (e.g., environment/cluster). Customers may require stronger SoD for operational vs security tasks.
- Private: Customer-controlled environment; RBAC still enforces least privilege within the platform, and customers control infrastructure/networking and can integrate with their IdP and logging systems.

Q: For Private deployments, can the customer bootstrap the first admin securely?
A: Yes. Private deployments include a secure bootstrap flow for establishing initial admin bindings, after which customers typically map IdP groups to roles to manage ongoing access. Bootstrap and subsequent privilege changes are auditable.

============================================================
NOTES / PLACEHOLDERS TO CONFIRM PER CUSTOMER
============================================================
- Confirm the customer’s required audit log retention window (e.g., 1 year / 7 years) and whether they require immutable storage.
- Confirm if they require explicit logging of all denied requests (some customers want it; some consider it noisy).
- Confirm whether they require “two-person rule” approvals for role/permission changes (Private deployment processes).
- Confirm if they require SCIM provisioning specifics (handled with Identity/IT).
- Provide sample audit log payload and SIEM field mapping under NDA.

Changelog (high-level)
- v0.7 (2025-03-06): added explicit “authorization decision context” fields and deny logging language; added Private bootstrap wording.
- v0.6 (2025-03-01): initial answer bank drafted from workshop notes and PRD.
